column1: # seance timestamp vectors -- UTC timestamp <TAB> seconds since the epoch.
# PROVENANCE, and the only reason this file is worth having: every epoch below
# was produced by date(1), on FreeBSD, as
# once, when this file was written, and then committed. seance's own converter
# is pure integer arithmetic (the days-from-civil algorithm) and never calls
# date(1) -- so these two implementations are genuinely independent, and this
# file is an oracle rather than a snapshot of the code's own opinion.
# tests/tier2/t_vectors.sh runs every row in both directions and does so under
# a non-UTC TZ and under two locales. A timestamp is UTC always, by spec, so
# any row that moves when the environment does is a defect and not a
# Lines beginning with '#' and blank lines are ignored.
# The rows are chosen for what a hand-rolled calendar gets wrong: the epoch
# itself and the seconds either side of it, pre-epoch instants, the leap-year
# century rules (1900 and 2100 are not leap years, 2000 is), the ends of
# months and years, and the 2038 signed-32-bit boundary.
# One row is deliberately absent. date(1) accepts 20260229T000000Z and returns
# 1772323200, which is 2026-03-01: 2026 is not a leap year and BSD date
# normalises the impossible date instead of refusing it. seance refuses it, so
# the two implementations disagree there on purpose and the case lives in
# snapnames.tsv as a "foreign" row rather than here as an epoch pair. That
# disagreement is the argument for not delegating validation to date(1) in the
# first place: a promotion must not read a replica whose name it had to guess
